title: Exposing Agents as MCP servers with mcp-agent: Sarmad Qadri

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The central thesis is that agents should be exposed as MCP servers, making MCP protocol design and agent-to-agent communication over MCP the primary subject. The mcp-agent framework is a developer tool for building agents and the demonstrated patterns are general-purpose rather than tied to a specific application vertical. The talk focuses on building and composing agent systems using MCP, not on production deployment or monitoring. Assumes familiarity with MCP concepts, agent patterns from Anthropic's Building Effective Agents, and workflow orchestration systems like Temporal. A conference presentation with a live coding demo of a multi-agent short-story grading workflow exposed as an MCP server. Multiple direct transcript quotes explicitly support MCP as the primary subject and the agents-as-MCP-servers protocol thesis.

summary: Sarmad Qadri draws on his experience with Language Server Protocol (LSP) at Microsoft to frame MCP as an analogous standardizing force for LLM-tool connectivity. He identifies three tech stack shifts enabling production agents in 2025: better models with reasoning and test-time compute, MCP as a universal standardized interface replacing fragmented platform-specific connectors, and simpler agent architectures replacing monolithic AI frameworks. He references Anthropic's Building Effective Agents blog post, describing patterns from augmented LLMs to evaluator-optimizer loops, fan-out/fan-in, and orchestrator-worker patterns. His framework mcp-agent implements all these patterns with three opinionated choices: MCP ubiquity across applications and services, agents as microservices deployable as MCP servers, and agents as asynchronous workflows with Temporal as durable execution backend. The core insight is that current agentic behavior lives only on the MCP client side, but if agents are themselves MCP servers, any MCP client can invoke, coordinate, and orchestrate them. This enables multi-agent collaboration over the base MCP protocol. The demo shows a short-story grading agent connecting to fetch and file system MCP servers, defining sub-agents (finder, writer, proofreader, fact checker, style enforcer) orchestrated by an orchestrator agent that generates a plan and executes it across about 100 lines of code. The workflow runs via Temporal, producing a graded report. Crucially, the same agent is then exposed as an MCP server itself, callable from Claude Desktop, which exposes workflows as tools, polls for status, and retrieves results asynchronously—demonstrating that the user could close the client and return later to check progress. This proves platform independence and the async workflow model where agents can be paused, retried, terminated, or await human feedback.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Sarmad introduces himself as CEO of Last Mile AI, drawing parallels between LSP's standardization of language services in IDEs and MCP's potential to standardize LLM-tool connectivity. He frames 2025 as the year agents hit production, with use cases like workflow automation, unstructured data processing, and information retrieval moving beyond proof-of-concept.

sections.title: The 2025 Agent Tech Stack
sections.summary: Three key changes: better models with reasoning and test-time compute shifting complexity into inference, MCP as a standardized interface adopted across major players, and simpler agent architectures replacing monolithic frameworks. References Anthropic's Building Effective Agents patterns: augmented LLM, evaluator-optimizer, fan-out/fan-in, and orchestrator-worker.

sections.title: mcp-agent Framework
sections.summary: Introduces mcp-agent, built during Christmas break, implementing all Building Effective Agents patterns with three opinionated choices: MCP everywhere, agents as microservices deployable as MCP servers, and agents as asynchronous workflows.

sections.title: Agents as MCP Servers
sections.summary: Core thesis: if agents are exposed as MCP servers, any MCP client can invoke and orchestrate them. Enables multi-agent communication over MCP protocol. Benefits: composable agents, platform-agnostic reuse, and scalable execution on dedicated infrastructure.

sections.title: Agents as Async Workflows and Demo Introduction
sections.summary: Agents should be modeled as async workflows because they can be paused, resumed, retried, await human feedback, or be triggered by webhooks or cron. Temporal is used as durable execution backend. Demo begins with a short-story grading agent task across proofreading, factual/logical consistency, and APA style adherence.

sections.title: Demo Execution and Agent-as-MCP-Server
sections.summary: The demo agent connects to fetch and file system MCP servers, defines sub-agents (finder, writer, proofreader, fact checker, style enforcer) orchestrated by an orchestrator that generates a plan and executes via Temporal in about 100 lines of code. The workflow produces a graded_report.md file. The agent is then exposed as an MCP server callable from Claude Desktop, which invokes it as a workflow, polls for completion status, and retrieves results—demonstrating async execution where the user could close the client and return later to check progress.

demonstrations: Demo shows a short-story grading agent connecting to fetch and file system MCP servers, defining sub-agents (finder, writer, proofreader, fact checker, style enforcer) orchestrated by an orchestrator that generates a plan and executes it via Temporal, producing a graded_report.md file across about 100 lines of code

Demo then exposes the same agent as an MCP server callable from Claude Desktop, which invokes it as a workflow, polls for status, and retrieves the graded report asynchronously—showing the user could close the client and return later
limitations: Currently agentic behavior exists only on the MCP client side, not server side
Many MCP servers today are just one-to-one mappings of existing REST API services to MCP tools
High-impact use cases have been stalled in proof-of-concept stage until now
quantitativeClaims: Demo workflow is about 100 lines of code
LSP resulted in hundreds of language servers available after standardizing the interface
